## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Parābhava Sutta* is the sixth discourse in the Uraga Vagga of the *Suttanipāta* (vv. 91–115, PTS Snp 18) [Norman 1983; Norman 1997–2001; Saddhatissa 2013]. Set at Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery in the Jeta Grove near Sāvatthī, the discourse is framed as a dialogue between the Buddha and an effulgent deity (*devatā*) who visits him late at night to ask about the causes of spiritual decline and failure in the world [Norman 1983; Saddhatissa 2013].

Regarded as the thematic counterpart or antithesis of the *Maṅgala Sutta*, the discourse details the attitudes and behaviors that lead to the downfall of a householder [Buddhist Forum 1994–96; Kalupahana 2001]. The Buddha explains that while love of the Dhamma leads to progress, hatred of the Dhamma leads to downfall [Kalupahana 2001]. The text proceeds to catalog specific causes of ruin, including indolence, bad companionship, neglect of elderly parents, deceit toward ascetics, arrogance rooted in wealth, and vices such as compulsive involvement with women, intoxicating drink, and gambling (*itthīdhutto*, *surādhutto*, *akkhadhutto*) [Sarath-Chandra 2007; Harris 2005]. Because of its practical social and ethical focus, the discourse is widely invoked alongside suttas such as the *Sigālovāda* and *Vyaggapajja*, and has been utilized by modern Buddhist welfare movements such as Sarvodaya in Sri Lanka [Sarath-Chandra 2007; Bond 1988].

Text-reuse analyses show significant overlap with canonical verse and opening formulaic passages across the Pali canon [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus registers 105 matching passages across 20 Pali texts, with extensive reuse in the *Devatā Saṁyutta* (SN 1), *Devaputta Saṁyutta* (SN 2), *Chakkanipāta* (AN 6), *Sattakanipāta* (AN 7), *Brahma Saṁyutta* (SN 6), and the *Maṅgala Sutta* (Snp 2.4), as well as citation in post-canonical anthologies such as the *Suttantanīti* [DharmaNexus]. Machine alignments also identify cross-linguistic correspondences in the Chinese *Bieyi za ahan jing* (T 100), as well as shared thematic citations in Tibetan translations of the *Śrāvakabhūmi* and *Saddharmānusmṛtyupasthāna* [DharmaNexus].
